title: The Suffering Servant: Wounded for Our Transgressions
summary: A group of speakers confesses that they despised the Servant, a man of sorrows with nothing attractive about him, and assumed God was punishing him, when in fact he was carrying their sicknesses and was crushed for their iniquities. Silent like a lamb, he is condemned, killed, and buried with the wicked, though he had done no violence. Yet it was the LORD's will: his life becomes a guilt offering, and after his anguish he sees light, justifies many, and is given a portion with the great because he bore the sin of many and interceded for transgressors.
story:
This is the heart of the fourth Servant Song, which began at 52:13. In the earlier songs the Servant was chosen to bring justice to the nations (42:1-4), called to restore Israel and be a light to the Gentiles (49:1-6), and beaten and spat upon for his faithfulness while he trusted God to vindicate him (50:4-9). Now his suffering is explained: it is not punishment for his own sin but the means by which others are healed and forgiven. Chapters 40 to 52 promised that Jerusalem's punishment was over and that the exiles would come home; chapter 53 shows how the deeper problem, sin itself, is dealt with.

The chapter is also the answer to a question the book has raised from its first page. Isaiah 1:5-6 pictured Israel as a body beaten from head to foot, with wounds and welts and open sores not bound up; here the same word for welts returns (verse 5), now on the Servant, and by them the many are healed. What follows in chapters 54 and 55 is the result: a barren city told to sing, an everlasting covenant of peace, and an open invitation to everyone who is thirsty. No chapter of the Old Testament has been read, argued over, or preached more by Jews and Christians alike, and none is quoted more directly in the New Testament's account of Jesus' death.
historical:
The song names no historical person, and that silence has driven more than two thousand years of interpretation. It belongs to Isaiah 40 to 55, chapters that speak to Jews exiled in Babylon: they announce that Jerusalem's punishment is over, mock Babylon's gods, and name Cyrus of Persia as the LORD's anointed who will let the exiles go home (44:28, 45:1). Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC. Most modern scholars assign these chapters to an unnamed prophet of the exile writing in the 540s BC, often called Second Isaiah; the traditional view, held by Jewish and Christian readers for most of history and defended by conservative scholars today, is that Isaiah of Jerusalem wrote the whole book in the eighth century BC and foresaw the exile (see the hard question on chapter 52). Either way the song was first heard by a people who knew national humiliation, deportation, and the question of whether suffering meant that God had abandoned them.

The text is well attested. The Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran (1QIsaa), found in 1947 and copied around 125 BC, contains the chapter essentially as we have it, with a handful of variants, the most important being ‘he will see light’ in verse 11, which a second Qumran scroll (1QIsab), a fragment from Cave 4 (4QIsad), and the Septuagint also read. The Septuagint, translated by Jews in Egypt in the last centuries BC, already shaped how Greek-speaking Jews and then Christians heard the song.

The earliest readings of the song are themselves historical evidence. Daniel 12:3, which most scholars date to the persecution under the Seleucid king Antiochus IV (167 to 164 BC) and traditional scholars to the sixth century BC, promises that the wise (maskilim, from the verb of 52:13) and those who lead many to righteousness (the phrase of 53:11) will shine like stars; H. L. Ginsberg argued in 1953 that this is the oldest surviving interpretation of the song. The Wisdom of Solomon, from Alexandria in the first century BC or the first century AD, tells of a righteous man who calls himself a child (pais) of God, is condemned to a shameful death, and is then exalted while his persecutors confess their error (Wisdom 2:12-20, 5:1-8); George Nickelsburg (Resurrection, Immortality, and Eternal Life in Intertestamental Judaism, 1972) showed how closely it follows the pattern of Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12. Jewish writings of the Maccabean era also express the hope that the deaths of the righteous might turn away God's wrath from the nation: the youngest of seven martyred brothers prays that God's anger might end through his death (2 Maccabees 7:37-38), and 4 Maccabees (17:21-22) speaks of the martyrs as a ransom for the nation's sin. The Targum of Isaiah, the Aramaic paraphrase read in synagogues and reaching its final form in the early centuries AD, calls the Servant of 52:13 the Messiah, but transfers most of the song's sufferings to Israel and the nations and gives the Messiah the triumph, including the rebuilding of the sanctuary profaned by the people's sins.
cultural:
Two assumptions of the ancient world stand behind verse 4. Serious illness and disfigurement were widely taken as signs of divine punishment. Job's friends argue exactly this (“Who, being innocent, has ever perished?”, Job 4:7), and the disciples ask Jesus whose sin caused a man's blindness (John 9:2). In Israel's law a person with a serious skin disease had to live outside the camp, with torn clothes and covered lip, crying ‘Unclean’ (Leviticus 13:45-46), and people turned their faces away from such a person. So when the speakers saw the Servant diseased and struck down, they concluded he was stricken by God. The shock of the song is that they were right that God was involved and wrong about why.

The language of sacrifice would have been familiar to every Israelite. The guilt offering of verse 10 (asham) was the sacrifice brought to make reparation for a wrong, especially a trespass against what belonged to God, and it was accompanied by restitution plus a fifth (Leviticus 5:14 to 6:7). Even the Philistines, returning the captured ark, sent golden objects as an asham to the God of Israel (1 Samuel 6:3-4). The lamb led to slaughter and the sheep before its shearers (verse 7) came from the pastoral life of Judah's hill country, where animals went to death and shearing without protest; Jeremiah had used the same image of himself (Jeremiah 11:19). The scapegoat of the Day of Atonement, which carried the people's iniquities into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:21-22), uses the same verb for bearing iniquity that runs through this song.

Burial mattered deeply in Israel. To lie in the family tomb was to be gathered to one's fathers; to be denied it was a final disgrace (1 Kings 13:22, Jeremiah 22:18-19). The law required that an executed criminal's body be buried the same day (Deuteronomy 21:22-23), and the Mishnah, codified around AD 200, records that such criminals were not buried with their ancestors but in two burial places kept by the court (m. Sanhedrin 6:5). The wealthy of Jerusalem, by contrast, carved elaborate rock-cut tombs; Isaiah 22:15-16 rebukes the royal steward Shebna for cutting himself one, and a tomb inscription from Silwan, across the Kidron from the city, now in the British Museum, belongs to a royal steward whose name ends in -yahu and whom many identify with him. Verse 9 describes a man assigned a grave among the wicked, yet with a rich man in his death. In 1968 a first-century ossuary found at Giv'at ha-Mivtar in Jerusalem held the heel bone of a crucified man, Yehohanan, with the nail still in it, evidence that a crucified man could be laid in a family tomb, as the Gospels say Jesus was laid in the new tomb of Joseph of Arimathea.
literary:
Taken with 52:13-15, the song falls into five stanzas of roughly three verses each: 52:13-15, 53:1-3, 4-6, 7-9, and 10-12. God speaks in the first and last stanzas (“My Servant” in 52:13 and 53:11), framing the whole; in the middle three an unnamed ‘we’ speaks, first recalling how they despised the Servant, then confessing what they now understand, and then describing his trial and death. David Clines (I, He, We and They: A Literary Approach to Isaiah 53, 1976) argued that the poem's power lies partly in the fact that it never names any of its pronouns, leaving the reader to find a place among the ‘we’. The frame is a reversal: exaltation announced (52:13), humiliation described (53:1-9), exaltation explained (53:10-12).

Verses 4 to 6 are the turning point, built on a sharp contrast between ‘he’ and ‘we’: he took our infirmities, we considered him stricken; he was pierced for our transgressions, we all like sheep have gone astray. The central stanza begins and ends with the whole group, kullanu, ‘all of us’, in the guilt and in the provision. The vocabulary of sin (pesha, transgression; avon, iniquity; chet, sin) and of bearing it (nasa, to lift or bear; saval, to carry a load) runs through every stanza, so that the song reads like a single sustained transfer of burden. Words also return in new senses: the choli (sickness) and makhovot (pains) of verse 3 become ‘our’ sicknesses and ‘our’ pains in verse 4; the crushing of verse 5 becomes the LORD's will in verse 10; the verb paga, used when the LORD made iniquity fall on him in verse 6, returns when he intercedes for transgressors in verse 12.

Whether the Servant actually dies is debated, since verses 8 and 9 speak of being cut off from the land of the living and buried, while verses 10 to 12 promise that he will see offspring and prolong his days. Most readers, Jewish and Christian, take this as death followed by vindication beyond it; R. N. Whybray (Thanksgiving for a Liberated Prophet, 1978) and some others argued that the language of death is metaphor for extreme suffering, from which the Servant was delivered. The song ends where it began, with the Servant exalted and dividing spoil, but now the reader knows the cost.

outline.t: Who has believed? The despised man of sorrows
The confession: he carried our sorrows, we went astray
Silent like a lamb, cut off and buried with the wicked
The LORD's will: a guilt offering, light, and a portion with the great

doctrines.note: The chapter describes one suffering in place of many: “He was pierced for our transgressions” (verse 5), “the LORD has laid upon Him the iniquity of us all” (verse 6), and his soul is made a guilt offering (verse 10). This is the Old Testament's fullest picture of vicarious suffering, and the church has read it as the key to the cross, though Christians describe the mechanism in more than one way.

“By His knowledge My righteous Servant will justify many, and He will bear their iniquities” (verse 11). The many are declared righteous not by their own record but because the righteous one carries their guilt, the logic Paul develops when he says Jesus was delivered over for our trespasses and raised for our justification (Romans 4:25).

The song overturns the assumption that suffering always proves God's displeasure with the sufferer. The Servant is innocent (verse 9) and his suffering is redemptive, and the church has found in him a Savior who knows sickness and rejection from the inside (Hebrews 4:15).

The Servant is not called king or messiah in the song, yet he is exalted, allotted a portion with the great, and brings righteousness to many, and the Targum of Isaiah names him the Messiah. The church confesses that Jesus the Messiah fulfills this role, joining the royal hopes of Isaiah 9 and 11 with the Servant's suffering.

After being cut off from the land of the living (verse 8) and buried (verse 9), the Servant sees offspring, prolongs his days, and sees light (verses 10 and 11). The song does not explain how, but it speaks of life beyond his death, and the New Testament reads that vindication as fulfilled when Christ was raised ‘according to the Scriptures’ (1 Corinthians 15:3-4).

words.note: Choli, sickness or disease, about twenty-four times. It is used of physical illness (Deuteronomy 7:15, of the diseases of Egypt; 2 Kings 1:2 and 8:8, of kings' illnesses) and, in Ecclesiastes 5:17 and 6:2, of affliction more broadly. Verse 3 calls the Servant ‘known by sickness’ (the BSB's “acquainted with grief”), and verse 4 says “He took on our infirmities”, using the same noun; the related verb returns in verse 10, ‘to cause him to suffer’, literally to make him sick. The Servant bears not only sin but its effects in human weakness, and Matthew 8:17 applies verse 4 to Jesus' healings, while the Septuagint had already rendered it as ‘our sins’.

Nasa, to lift, carry, or bear, one of the commonest verbs in the Old Testament (about 650 times). With avon or chet (iniquity or sin) as its object it has two great senses. A person who ‘bears his iniquity’ carries its guilt and consequences (Leviticus 5:1, 17), and the scapegoat ‘bears’ the people's iniquities into the wilderness (Leviticus 16:22). But God ‘bearing iniquity’ means forgiving it: he is the one who forgives, literally lifts, iniquity, transgression, and sin (Exodus 34:7, Psalm 32:5). In verses 4 and 12 the Servant ‘bore’ our sicknesses and the sin of many: he carries what is lifted from others.

Saval, to carry a heavy load, found only about nine times, and its noun is used of the forced labor of porters (1 Kings 5:15). In Isaiah 46:4 God says he has made his people and will carry them, while Babylon's gods must be carried by their worshipers (46:7). In Lamentations 5:7 the survivors of Jerusalem say their fathers sinned and are no more, and ‘we bear their iniquities’, using this verb. The Servant takes that weight: “carried our sorrows” (verse 4) and “He will bear their iniquities” (verse 11).

Avon, iniquity, about 230 times. The standard lexicons show a range that English cannot hold in one word: the crooked act itself, the guilt that follows it, and the punishment it brings. Cain says ‘my avon is greater than I can bear’ (Genesis 4:13), which can mean his sin or his punishment. The song uses the word three times (verses 5, 6, and 11): he was crushed for our iniquities, the LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all, and he will bear their iniquities. The range matters for the chapter's meaning, since the Servant carries not only the consequences of wrong but the guilt itself.

Asham, guilt or the guilt offering, about forty-six times, twenty-seven of them in Leviticus. As a sacrifice (Leviticus 5:14 to 6:7, 7:1-7) the asham was offered when someone had trespassed against the LORD's holy things or wronged a neighbor, and it was joined to restitution plus a fifth; it dealt with a debt of wrong, not only with impurity. Calling the Servant's life an asham (verse 10) interprets his death in the terms of Israel's sacrificial system as a payment that repairs a real wrong before God, which is the move Hebrews makes at length (Hebrews 9:11-14, 10:10-14).

Tsadaq, to be righteous or in the right, about forty times, seventeen of them in Job, where the question is whether a man can be in the right before God (Job 9:2, 25:4). The Hiphil stem, used in verse 11, is legal: to declare someone in the right, to acquit. Judges must ‘justify the righteous and condemn the wicked’ (Deuteronomy 25:1), and Isaiah 5:23 condemns those who acquit the guilty for a bribe. That background is what makes verse 11 startling: the righteous Servant justifies the many, not by overlooking their guilt, but by bearing their iniquities. Daniel 12:3 uses the same form of those who lead many to righteousness.

Paga, to meet, encounter, strike, or entreat, about forty-six times. It is used of an attacker falling on someone (1 Kings 2:25-34, where Benaiah strikes down Joab and others), of boundaries meeting (Joshua 16:7), and of pleading with someone (Genesis 23:8, Ruth 1:16, Jeremiah 7:16). The song uses it at two decisive points: the LORD caused the iniquity of us all to fall on the Servant (verse 6), and the Servant makes intercession for the transgressors (verse 12). The one on whom guilt was made to fall makes his plea fall on God's ear for the guilty.

Chabburah, a welt, bruise, or stripe, the mark a blow leaves, only seven times in the Old Testament. It appears in the law of injury, ‘stripe for stripe’ (Exodus 21:25), in Lamech's boast (Genesis 4:23), and in Psalm 38:5, where the psalmist's wounds fester because of his folly. Isaiah 1:6 pictured the whole nation as covered with such welts, untended. Verse 5 turns the image around: “by His stripes we are healed”, the singular noun used collectively for the marks of his beating. First Peter 2:24 quotes the line to Christian slaves whose own backs bore such marks.

christ:
No Old Testament passage is used more directly of Jesus' death. At the Last Supper Jesus quotes verse 12, ‘He was numbered with the transgressors’, and says it must be fulfilled in him (Luke 22:37), the only direct quotation of this chapter attributed to Jesus in the Gospels; hours later he is crucified between two criminals (Luke 23:32-33). His saying that the Son of Man came “to give His life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45) is widely heard as an echo of the song's ‘many’. In Acts 8:26-35 an Ethiopian official is reading verses 7 and 8 in his chariot and asks, “who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?” (Acts 8:34); Philip begins from this Scripture and tells him the good news about Jesus. First Peter 2:21-25 weaves the chapter into its account of Christ's suffering: he committed no sin and no deceit was found in his mouth (verse 9), he did not retaliate when he suffered (verse 7), “He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree” (verses 4 and 12), by his stripes you are healed (verse 5), and you were like sheep going astray (verse 6).

The other writers draw on it too. John 12:38 and Romans 10:16 quote verse 1 of those who did not believe the report; Matthew 8:17 applies verse 4 to Jesus' healings; Paul says Jesus “was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification” (Romans 4:25) and that through the obedience of one man the many will be made righteous (Romans 5:19), both echoing verses 11 and 12; Hebrews says “Christ was offered once to bear the sins of many” (Hebrews 9:28). Philippians 2:6-11 follows the song's shape: the one who took the form of a servant humbled himself to death and was therefore exalted. The Gospels note Jesus' silence before the high priest and before Pilate (Mark 14:61, 15:5), and Matthew alone calls Joseph of Arimathea, in whose new tomb Jesus was laid, a rich man (Matthew 27:57-60); the Gospel writers do not cite Isaiah at that point, but Christian readers since the early church have noticed the correspondence with verse 9. John the Baptist's words, “Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29), may draw on verse 7 as well as on the Passover.

The New Testament's reading does not erase the song's first horizon. The Servant in Isaiah is called Israel (49:3) and has a mission to Israel (49:5-6); Christian theology has held these together by confessing Jesus as the true Israel, who does as one person what the nation was called to do, and who bears as the sinless one the sin of the many. The church confesses that in his death and resurrection God himself, in the person of the Son, bore the cost of human sin and was vindicated, so that by his wounds we are healed.
interpretation:
The earliest Christian writers quoted the whole song. Clement of Rome (1 Clement 16, around AD 96) cites 53:1-12 in the Greek to hold up Christ's humility, and Justin Martyr quotes it in his First Apology (chapters 50 and 51) and debates it with Trypho. Origen (Against Celsus 1.55) reports that a Jewish teacher told him the song spoke of the whole people, scattered and afflicted, as one person. Augustine (City of God 18.29) reads the song as the Father speaking of Christ. Jewish tradition kept more than one reading. The Targum names the Servant the Messiah while reassigning the suffering; the Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 98b) records rabbis who called the Messiah ‘the leper’ from verse 4, and Moed Katan 28a teaches that the death of the righteous atones. From the eleventh century the collective reading became standard in the great commentaries: Rashi, Abraham Ibn Ezra, and David Kimhi took the Servant as Israel and the ‘we’ as the nations who misjudged it, and Ibn Ezra reports Saadia Gaon's view that the Servant was Jeremiah. The Dominican Raymond Martini gathered the older messianic rabbinic readings for Christian polemic in his Pugio Fidei (after 1278), and the Karaite Isaac of Troki answered Christian arguments with the collective reading in Hizzuk Emunah (late sixteenth century). Adolf Neubauer and S. R. Driver collected the Jewish commentaries in The Fifty-Third Chapter of Isaiah According to the Jewish Interpreters (1876 and 1877). Amy-Jill Levine and Marc Zvi Brettler (The Bible With and Without Jesus, 2020) argue that ancient Jewish readers mostly took the Servant as an individual, and that the national reading came to dominate in the Middle Ages.

The Reformers made the song central to their preaching of the cross. Luther lectured on it more than once, and his exposition of Isaiah 53 dates from the 1540s; Calvin preached seven sermons on 52:13 to 53:12 in Geneva in the summer of 1558, published the same year. Modern critical study began with Bernhard Duhm (1892), who isolated the four Servant Songs. Christopher North's The Suffering Servant in Deutero-Isaiah (1948) surveyed the identifications; Morna Hooker's Jesus and the Servant (1959) doubted that Jesus himself drew on the song, against Joachim Jeremias; Harry Orlinsky (1967) and R. N. Whybray (1978) denied that the song teaches vicarious suffering. Bernd Janowski and Peter Stuhlmacher's collection The Suffering Servant: Isaiah 53 in Jewish and Christian Sources (English 2004) traces the whole history.

The Revised Common Lectionary reads 52:13 to 53:12 on Good Friday in all three years, while the synagogue's cycle of consolation readings passes from 52:12 to 54:1. Handel's Messiah (1742) gives the song the heart of Part Two: the alto aria He was despised and the choruses Surely he hath borne our griefs, And with his stripes we are healed, and All we like sheep have gone astray, the last reworked from the same Italian duet as For unto us. Philip Bliss's hymn Man of Sorrows (1875), and the late medieval image of Christ as Man of Sorrows showing his wounds, take their name from verse 3.
text:
The Hebrew of this chapter is difficult in places, and English Bibles differ. In verse 3 the phrase rendered “rejected by men” can mean ‘ceasing from among men’ or ‘the frailest of men’, and “acquainted with grief” is literally ‘known by sickness’. In verse 4 the Septuagint reads ‘he bears our sins and suffers pain for us’, spiritualizing the Hebrew's sicknesses and pains; Matthew 8:17 follows the Hebrew more closely, while 1 Peter follows the Greek. In verse 8 the Hebrew phrase about ‘his generation’ can be rendered ‘as for his generation, who considered’ (RSV, ESV), “who can recount His descendants” (BSB), or ‘who shall declare his generation’ (KJV); the Septuagint's form, ‘who will describe his generation?’, was read by the church fathers as a reference to the mystery of the Son's origin. The last word of verse 8, lamo (‘to them’ or ‘to him’), is read by the Septuagint as ‘to death’, a difference of one letter, and the choice matters for whether the stroke falls on an individual or a group.

In verse 9 the Great Isaiah Scroll spells ‘in his death’ with an extra letter, which some scholars read as ‘his burial mound’, and many modern scholars emend ‘a rich man’ to ‘evildoers’ for a closer parallel, without manuscript support; the Septuagint reads ‘I will give the wicked for his burial and the rich for his death’. In verse 10 the key clause can be read as addressed to God (‘when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin’, KJV) or with his soul as subject (‘when his soul makes an offering for guilt’, ESV); the BSB's passive leaves the agent open. In verse 11 the Masoretic Text has ‘he will see’ with no object, while 1QIsaa, 1QIsab, 4QIsad, and the Septuagint read ‘he will see light’, which the NIV, NRSV, ESV, and BSB adopt and the KJV does not. In verse 12 the opening clauses can mean ‘I will give him a portion among the great’ or ‘I will give him the many as his portion’. Mark 15:28, which cites verse 12 at the crucifixion in the KJV, is absent from the earliest manuscripts of Mark and is omitted or footnoted in most modern versions. Chapter and verse numbering is the same in Hebrew and English Bibles.

teach.big: The Servant whom everyone despised and thought God had rejected was in fact bearing their sins and sicknesses by God's will, so that through his wounds, death, and vindication many are healed, made righteous, and prayed for.

outline.t: God's saving power arrived in a form no one expected or admired, and the right response begins with confessing that we did not believe the report and did not esteem him.
What we took for God's judgment on him was God's provision for us: he carried our sicknesses and was crushed for our sins, and all of us, each in our own way, are the sheep that strayed.
He went to an unjust death willingly and silently, though innocent in deed and word, and was given a criminal's grave, yet with a rich man in his death.

Behind the injustice stood God's purpose: his life became a guilt offering, and beyond death he sees light, justifies the many by bearing their iniquities, and intercedes for the very transgressors among whom he was counted.

teach.pitfalls:
Three misuses are common. The first reduces the chapter to proof texting, a list of predictions checked off against the Gospels, without teaching the poem's own movement from misjudgment to confession. The song's power lies in the ‘we’ who were wrong and now say so; teachers should invite the room into that confession rather than only arguing its fulfillment. The second is to claim, on the strength of verse 5 and Matthew 8:17, that Christ's death guarantees physical healing now to everyone with enough faith. The New Testament does apply verse 4 to Jesus' healings, and Christians rightly pray for healing, but 1 Peter 2:24 applies the healing of verse 5 above all to forgiveness and new life, and Paul, Timothy, and Trophimus were not always healed (2 Corinthians 12:7-9, 1 Timothy 5:23, 2 Timothy 4:20). Promising otherwise wounds the sick.

The third is to flatten the debate over the Servant's identity. Teachers should not caricature the Jewish collective reading, which has real support in Isaiah's own naming of Israel as God's servant, nor imply that all Jewish interpreters rejected a messianic reading, since the Targum and the Talmud show otherwise. Nor should Christians forget that the chapter was used for centuries as a weapon in forced disputations against Jews; it should be taught with the same humility the ‘we’ of the song displays. Finally, in explaining the atonement, avoid pitting the Father against the Son, as if a reluctant victim were seized by an angry God. The song presents the Servant pouring out his own life (verse 12) and the LORD's purpose standing behind it (verse 10), and the Christian confession is that the Son freely gave himself in the one will of the triune God.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on many in a congregation: the chronically ill, the disfigured, those who have been despised and treated as cursed, the grieving, and those who have been abused. Teach that the Servant's suffering was not proof of God's rejection, and that the same false conclusion should not be drawn about anyone's illness or misfortune. Be especially careful with verse 7. The Servant's silence was his free choice for the sake of others, not a model that requires victims to endure abuse quietly; the chapter itself calls his treatment oppression and injustice (verse 8), and victims of abuse should be encouraged to seek safety, speak, and seek justice. For those burdened by guilt or scrupulosity, verses 5, 6, and 11 are among the Bible's clearest assurances that the iniquity of us all was laid on him, and that he still intercedes for transgressors.

hard.q: Who is the Servant: Israel, the prophet, or the Messiah Jesus?
hard.a:
The Ethiopian's question in Acts 8:34 is still the first question, and the strongest non-Christian answer deserves to be heard first. Isaiah itself repeatedly names Israel as God's servant: “But you, O Israel, My servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen” (41:8; also 44:1-2, 45:4, 48:20), and in one of the Servant Songs, “You are My Servant, Israel, in whom I will display My glory” (49:3). On this reading, held by Rashi, Ibn Ezra, and David Kimhi, argued against Christian polemic by Isaac of Troki, and maintained by most Jewish interpreters today, the Servant is the people of Israel, humiliated and scattered among the nations, and the ‘we’ are the nations and their kings (52:15) who finally recognize that Israel suffered unjustly and that its suffering served their good. A related view limits the Servant to the faithful remnant within Israel. Others take him as an individual of the prophet's own day: the prophet himself (R. N. Whybray), a figure like Jeremiah, whose language of a lamb led to slaughter and of being cut off from the land of the living is close to this song (Jeremiah 11:19; Saadia Gaon held this view), or a leader of the exiles. Harry Orlinsky argued that the song describes a prophet's sufferings and does not teach vicarious atonement at all. Critical scholars, Jewish and Christian, add that reading the song as a detailed prediction of Jesus lifts it out of its setting in the Babylonian exile.

Christian interpreters answer that the Servant of this song cannot simply be the nation. In 49:5-6 the Servant has a mission to restore Jacob and gather Israel, so he is distinguished from Israel even while bearing its name. He suffers without sin (53:9), while the nation in these chapters suffers for its sins (40:2, 42:24-25, 50:1). His suffering is voluntary (53:7, 12) and substitutionary, ‘for the transgression of My people’ (53:8), which is hard to say of Israel if the people in question are Israel. And the song's language of a single man, grave, and offspring is intensely individual. Christopher North (1948), after surveying every proposal, concluded that the Servant is best understood as an individual figure. Many Christian scholars also hold that the collective and individual readings belong together: the Servant is Israel as God meant it to be, and the song describes one person who embodies Israel's vocation and does for Israel and the nations what the nation could not do. The New Testament identifies that person as Jesus. Jewish readers also point out, fairly, that ancient Jewish tradition itself read the song messianically in places (the Targum, Sanhedrin 98b), though not as a portrait of a dying Messiah who atones; Levine and Brettler note that some ancient readings were individual as well. The question of the Servant's identity is where Jews and Christians most sharply part, and each tradition's answer is tied to what it confesses about the Messiah.

hard.q: How can it be just for one person's suffering to take away another's sin?
hard.a:
The moral objection is ancient and serious. The prophets themselves insist that each person bears his own guilt: “The soul who sins is the one who will die. A son will not bear the iniquity of his father” (Ezekiel 18:20; compare Deuteronomy 24:16). When Moses offered to be blotted out of God's book for Israel's sin (Exodus 32:32), God refused. Faustus Socinus (On Jesus Christ the Savior, written 1578, published 1594) argued that guilt and merit cannot be transferred from one person to another, that a God who forgives freely needs no satisfaction, and that punishing the innocent in place of the guilty is contrary to justice. In the twentieth century feminist theologians Joanne Carlson Brown and Rebecca Parker (For God So Loved the World?, 1989) argued that doctrines of redemptive suffering picture God as an abusive father and teach victims to accept abuse, and Steve Chalke (The Lost Message of Jesus, 2003) warned that some preaching of penal substitution makes the cross look like cosmic child abuse. Jewish interpreters add that the Hebrew Bible nowhere else makes a human life a sacrifice for sin, and Orlinsky and Whybray denied that the song teaches substitution at all.

The responses begin with the song itself. The Servant is not a third party seized against his will: he pours out his life (verse 12), goes silently and willingly (verse 7), and makes intercession for the transgressors. The song also presents the LORD's own purpose standing behind his suffering (verse 10), while calling the human process that killed him oppression and injustice (verse 8). Jewish tradition itself knew the idea that the suffering of the righteous can benefit others: the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 7 and 4 Maccabees 17 and the Talmud's teaching that the death of the righteous atones (Moed Katan 28a). Anselm of Canterbury (Why God Became Man, 1098) argued that only one who is both God and man could make satisfaction, and John Stott (The Cross of Christ, 1986) answered the objection of injustice by insisting that God does not punish a reluctant third party but substitutes himself in the person of his Son. Fleming Rutledge (The Crucifixion, 2015) argues that the cross must be understood through many biblical images at once, including substitution, victory over the powers, and sacrifice, and that removing substitution loses something the Bible insists on. Christians who emphasize Christ's victory over sin and death (the view Gustaf Aulén called Christus Victor in 1931) or his representative obedience and our union with him read the same chapter with a different emphasis. The church confesses that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3); how best to explain the mechanism of that ‘for’ is a question on which faithful Christians continue to differ.

observe: Who speaks in 52:13-15 and 53:11-12, and who speaks in 53:1-9? How does the ‘we’ describe their earlier view of the Servant?
List every verb in verses 4 to 6 and 11 to 12 that describes the Servant carrying or bearing something. What does he carry?
What does the song say about the Servant's innocence (verse 9), his silence (verse 7), and what happens to him after his death (verses 10 to 12)?
interpret: Why did the speakers conclude that the Servant was ‘stricken by God’ (verse 4), and what did they learn that changed their minds?
Verse 10 says it was the LORD's will to crush him, and verse 8 calls his death injustice. How can both be true?
What does it mean that the righteous Servant will ‘justify many’ by bearing their iniquities (verse 11)?
apply: The speakers say “we esteemed Him not.” When have you misjudged someone's suffering, or had your own misjudged?
Verse 6 says “We all like sheep have gone astray, each one has turned to his own way.” What is ‘your own way’, and what does it mean that the LORD laid that iniquity on him?
The song ends with the Servant praying for transgressors. How does that change the way you pray for those who have wronged you?
